desk.name: Combustion Reactions
desk.description: Select a fuel and a supporter/test reagent to explore combustion chemistry — complete and incomplete burning, flame colours, metal combustions, limewater tests, and soot formation.

chemicals.name: Magnesium Ribbon
chemicals.hazard: burns_bright_white — never look directly at flame

chemicals.name: Methane Gas
chemicals.hazard: flammable_gas — no naked flames near cylinder

chemicals.name: Cobalt Chloride Paper
chemicals.hazard: mild — cobalt compounds are slightly toxic

reactions.name: Magnesium Burning in Oxygen — Dazzling White Flame

output.observation: Magnesium burns with an intensely bright white flame. Dense white smoke of magnesium oxide fills the gas jar. A white powdery ash (MgO) is left behind.

reactions.educational_note: Magnesium undergoes complete combustion in oxygen. The product MgO is a white solid. This is also a synthesis (combination) reaction. NEVER look directly at the flame — it emits UV radiation.

reactions.name: Magnesium Ash + Limewater — No Reaction
reactions.formula: MgO + Ca(OH)2 -> no reaction (MgO is insoluble)

output.observation: Magnesium ribbon does not react with limewater at room temperature. Limewater stays clear. The two do not combust together.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater is a test reagent for CO2, not a combustion supporter. Metals require an ignition source and oxygen to combust — not limewater.

reactions.name: Magnesium + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Mg + CoCl2 paper -> no combustion reaction

output.observation: No combustion reaction. Cobalt chloride paper is a moisture-detection test reagent, not a fuel or oxidant. No reaction occurs.

reactions.educational_note: Cobalt chloride paper tests for water (turns pink when wet). It does not support or cause combustion.

reactions.name: Magnesium Burns with Copper(II) Oxide — Displacement

output.observation: Vigorous reaction with bright sparks and intense heat. Reddish-brown copper metal is seen in the white ash. MgO white powder also forms.

reactions.educational_note: Magnesium displaces copper from copper oxide because Mg is more reactive than Cu. This is both a combustion-type and a displacement reaction. The reddish product confirms copper metal formation.

reactions.name: Sulfur Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, Choking Fumes

output.odor: pungent choking smell — rotten eggs / matchstick
output.observation: Sulfur burns with a beautiful pale blue flame. Dense, choking white-gray fumes of SO2 fill the gas jar. The fumes smell strongly of burning matchsticks.

reactions.educational_note: Sulfur combustion produces sulfur dioxide (SO2), an acidic gas responsible for acid rain. In a fume cupboard, SO2 can be tested by its bleaching of damp litmus paper.

reactions.name: SO2 + Limewater — Turns Milky

output.observation: Limewater turns milky white — indicating an acidic gas. Note: SO2 gives the same limewater test as CO2, so further tests are needed to distinguish them.

reactions.educational_note: SO2 makes limewater milky (just like CO2 does). Additional tests (e.g. bleaching of potassium manganate) can distinguish SO2 from CO2. Both are acidic gases.

reactions.name: Sulfur + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Relevant Test

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper tests for water. Sulfur combustion produces SO2, not water — so the paper stays blue. No water is produced when sulfur burns.

reactions.educational_note: Only fuels containing hydrogen (H) produce water when burned. Sulfur contains no hydrogen, so no water forms and cobalt chloride paper does not change colour.

reactions.name: Sulfur + Copper(II) Oxide — No Direct Combustion
reactions.formula: S + CuO -> no clean combustion at room temperature

output.observation: No reaction at room temperature. Sulfur and copper oxide do not combust together without very high heat input. This pair is not used in a standard combustion experiment.

reactions.educational_note: Not all pairs of combustible and oxidising materials react under normal lab conditions. Activation energy and reactivity must both be sufficient.

reactions.name: Carbon (Charcoal) Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, CO2

output.observation: Charcoal glows orange-red and burns cleanly in pure oxygen. No visible smoke. Colourless, odourless CO2 is produced. The glow intensifies in pure O2 compared to air.

reactions.educational_note: Complete combustion of carbon gives CO2. If oxygen is limited, incomplete combustion gives CO (carbon monoxide), a colourless, odourless, and very toxic gas.

reactions.name: CO2 Test — Limewater Turns Milky

output.observation: Limewater turns milky white — the classic positive test for carbon dioxide. The white precipitate is calcium carbonate (chalk).

reactions.educational_note: The limewater test is the standard school test for CO2. Milky = CO2 present. If excess CO2 is bubbled through, the precipitate can redissolve forming Ca(HCO3)2.

reactions.name: Carbon Combustion + Cobalt Chloride Paper — Stays Blue

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — confirming that carbon combustion produces no water. Carbon has no hydrogen, so no H2O can form.

reactions.educational_note: Only hydrogen-containing fuels produce water on combustion. Pure carbon produces only CO2 (complete) or CO (incomplete). Cobalt chloride paper stays blue = no water.

reactions.name: Carbon Reduces Copper Oxide — Reddish Copper Appears

output.observation: Black copper oxide slowly turns reddish-brown as copper metal is produced. CO2 gas is also produced (confirmed by limewater). Carbon acts as a reducing agent.

reactions.educational_note: Carbon reduces copper oxide — a key industrial concept (blast furnace). Carbon is oxidised to CO2; copper oxide is reduced to copper. This is a redox reaction.

reactions.name: Ethanol Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, CO2 + H2O

output.odor: faint sweet alcoholic smell near base of flame
output.observation: Ethanol burns with a near-invisible pale blue flame. No smoke or soot. Water condenses on a cool surface held above the flame. CO2 can be confirmed with limewater.

reactions.educational_note: Ethanol is a clean-burning alcohol fuel. The products are CO2 and water — same as any complete hydrocarbon combustion. Its almost invisible flame is a lab safety hazard.

reactions.name: Ethanol Combustion Products — CO2 Turns Limewater Milky
reactions.formula: CO2 (from C2H5OH combustion) + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCO3 + H2O

output.observation: Combustion products of ethanol are bubbled through limewater. It turns milky white — confirming CO2 was produced by the ethanol burning.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater confirms CO2 in ethanol combustion products. This is a key practical skill: using a delivery tube to divert combustion gases through limewater.

reactions.name: Ethanol Combustion — Water Detected by Cobalt Chloride Paper

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper turns from blue to pink when held in the water vapour produced by burning ethanol. This confirms water (H2O) is a product of combustion.

reactions.educational_note: Blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink in the presence of water. This is the standard water test. Ethanol contains hydrogen, so burning it always produces water.

reactions.name: Ethanol + Copper Oxide — No Direct Combustion at Room Temperature

output.observation: No reaction at room temperature. Ethanol requires ignition to combust. Copper oxide is not an ignition source — it is an oxidising solid that requires high temperatures.

reactions.educational_note: Combustion needs three things: fuel, oxygen, and sufficient activation energy (ignition). Just mixing ethanol and CuO does not trigger a reaction without heat.

reactions.name: Candle Wax Burns in Oxygen — Yellow Flame, CO2 + H2O

output.observation: Candle wax burns with a bright yellow-orange flame in pure oxygen. No soot. Water vapour and CO2 are produced. The flame is much brighter in pure O2 than in air.

reactions.educational_note: Complete combustion of paraffin wax produces only CO2 and H2O. The yellow colour of a candle flame in air is due to incandescent soot particles — absent in pure oxygen.

reactions.name: Candle Combustion Products — CO2 Turns Limewater Milky

output.observation: Limewater turns milky white as candle combustion gases are bubbled through. Positive test for CO2. The white precipitate is calcium carbonate (the same as chalk).

reactions.educational_note: This is the classic school limewater test for CO2 using a burning candle. Milky white result = CO2 confirmed. Used to prove that hydrocarbons contain carbon.

reactions.name: Candle Combustion — Water Detected by Cobalt Chloride Paper
reactions.formula: C25H52 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O (water turns paper pink)

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper held above a burning candle turns from blue to pink — confirming water vapour is produced by combustion. You may also see water droplets condense.

reactions.educational_note: The candle + cobalt chloride paper test is a standard practical. Pink = water. This proves that paraffin wax contains hydrogen — since only H-containing fuels make water.

reactions.name: Candle Wax + Copper Oxide — No Room Temperature Reaction

output.observation: No reaction at room temperature. Candle wax is a fuel that needs a flame to ignite. Copper oxide does not act as an ignition source under these conditions.

reactions.educational_note: The fire triangle (fuel, oxygen, heat) applies here. Wax + CuO have fuel and an oxidant but no ignition source — so no combustion occurs.

reactions.name: Methane Burns in Oxygen — Blue Flame, CO2 + H2O

output.odor: odorless (methane) — slight smell from odorant added in domestic supply
output.observation: Methane burns with a clean bright blue flame in pure oxygen — no soot or smoke. CO2 and water vapour are produced. This is the cleanest burning fossil fuel.

reactions.educational_note: Complete combustion of methane (natural gas / Bunsen burner fuel): CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. The blue flame indicates complete combustion; a yellow flame indicates incomplete combustion.

reactions.name: Methane Combustion — CO2 Turns Limewater Milky

output.observation: Methane combustion gases are passed through limewater. It turns milky white — confirming CO2 was produced. The Bunsen burner itself uses this reaction.

reactions.educational_note: The limewater test works for all carbon-containing fuels. Methane from the Bunsen burner produces CO2 that turns limewater milky.

reactions.name: Methane Combustion — Water Detected by Cobalt Chloride Paper

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper turns pink when held in methane combustion gases — confirming water vapour production. Methane (CH4) has 4 hydrogen atoms, all converted to water.

reactions.educational_note: Methane has 4 hydrogen atoms → 2 water molecules per CH4 burned. Cobalt chloride paper is a quick, easy water test used alongside limewater in combustion practicals.

reactions.name: Methane + Copper Oxide — Slow Reduction at High Temperature

output.observation: When methane gas is passed over heated copper oxide, the black CuO slowly turns reddish-brown as copper metal is formed. CO2 and water vapour are also produced.

reactions.educational_note: Methane reduces copper oxide at high temperatures — a redox reaction. CuO is reduced to Cu (gains electrons); CH4 is oxidised to CO2 + H2O. Used in industry to reduce metal oxides.

reactions.name: Iron Wool Burns in Oxygen — Glowing Sparks

output.observation: Iron wool glows and showers brilliant orange sparks in pure oxygen. Black-brown iron oxide ash forms. The sparks are a dramatic and memorable demonstration.

reactions.educational_note: Iron burns in pure oxygen but not in air (too slow — it only rusts). The product Fe3O4 is magnetic. This shows that combustion supports vary in how vigorously they react.

reactions.name: Iron + Limewater — No Reaction

output.observation: No reaction. Iron does not react with limewater at room temperature. Limewater is a CO2 test reagent — iron combustion produces no CO2.

reactions.educational_note: Iron combustion produces iron oxide — not CO2. So limewater stays clear. This is a useful contrast: metal combustion ≠ CO2 production.

reactions.name: Iron + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Water Produced

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — iron combustion produces no water. Iron contains no hydrogen, so water cannot be a product.

reactions.educational_note: Metals produce metal oxides when burned — not CO2 or H2O. These are key differences from hydrocarbon combustion. Cobalt chloride paper = no change confirms no water.

reactions.name: Iron + Copper Oxide — Displacement (Thermite Type)

output.observation: When heated strongly, iron displaces copper from copper oxide. Reddish-brown copper is seen in the residue alongside black iron oxide.

reactions.educational_note: Iron is higher in the reactivity series than copper, so it displaces copper from CuO. This requires strong heating — not a room temperature reaction. Iron is oxidised; copper is reduced.

reactions.name: Calcium Burns in Oxygen — Red-Orange Flame

output.ash_name: Calcium Oxide (CaO) — white, reacts with water to form Ca(OH)2
output.observation: Calcium burns with a vivid brick-red / orange flame in oxygen. White calcium oxide smoke is produced. The ash (CaO) fizzes and heats up when water is added.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium burns more vigorously than iron but less vigorously than magnesium. CaO (quicklime) is industrially important — mixed with water it forms Ca(OH)2 (slaked lime / limewater).

reactions.name: Calcium Oxide Ash + Limewater — No CO2 Test Reaction
reactions.formula: CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2 (quicklime reacts with water in limewater)

output.observation: Calcium oxide (formed from burning calcium) reacts exothermically with water in the limewater. The mixture heats up. This is not a CO2 detection — it is CaO + H2O.

reactions.educational_note: CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2 (limewater) is an important reaction used industrially. However, this does not test for CO2. Only CO2 turns limewater milky by forming CaCO3.

reactions.name: Calcium Combustion — Cobalt Chloride Paper Stays Blue

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — calcium combustion produces no water. Calcium (Ca) has no hydrogen, so H2O cannot be a product.

reactions.educational_note: Metal combustion products are always metal oxides — never CO2 or H2O. Cobalt chloride paper confirms no water in metal combustion. A key distinction from hydrocarbon combustion.

reactions.name: Calcium + Copper Oxide — Calcium Displaces Copper

output.observation: Vigorous exothermic reaction with sparks and heat. Reddish-brown copper and white CaO are formed. Calcium is more reactive than copper and displaces it from its oxide.

reactions.educational_note: Calcium is high in the reactivity series (above copper), so it easily reduces CuO. This demonstrates the reactivity series through a combustion-type displacement.

reactions.name: Oxygen + Limewater — No Reaction

output.observation: Oxygen gas bubbled through limewater causes no change. Limewater only turns milky with CO2 or SO2 — not with O2.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater is a selective reagent — it tests for acidic gases like CO2 and SO2, not for oxygen. Oxygen is neutral and does not react with Ca(OH)2.

reactions.name: Oxygen + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Reaction
reactions.formula: O2 + CoCl2 paper -> no reaction (no water present)

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper stays blue — pure oxygen gas contains no water, so no colour change. Oxygen itself is an oxidant, not a source of water.

reactions.educational_note: Cobalt chloride paper only responds to water (H2O). Pure dry oxygen gas doesn't contain H2O, so the paper stays blue. The test is simple: pink = water, blue = dry.

reactions.name: Oxygen + Copper Oxide — No Further Reaction
reactions.formula: O2 + CuO -> no reaction (CuO is already fully oxidised)

output.observation: No reaction. Copper oxide (CuO) is already fully oxidised — copper is in its +2 state and cannot be oxidised further by oxygen under normal conditions.

reactions.educational_note: CuO is a stable, fully oxidised compound. Oxygen cannot react further with it. This is why CuO is used as an oxidant in reduction reactions — it easily gives up its oxygen to fuels.

reactions.name: Limewater + Cobalt Chloride Paper — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Ca(OH)2 (aq) + CoCl2 paper -> no chemical reaction

output.observation: Cobalt chloride paper turns pink — but only because limewater is an aqueous solution (it contains water). This is not a combustion reaction; it is just moisture detection.

reactions.educational_note: Limewater is a solution, so it contains water. Cobalt chloride paper detects that water. Important: this does not confirm combustion products — it just shows the reagent itself is wet.

reactions.name: Limewater + Copper Oxide — No Reaction
reactions.formula: Ca(OH)2 + CuO -> no reaction at room temperature

output.observation: No significant reaction at room temperature. Limewater and copper oxide are both reagents/products of combustion reactions — they do not react with each other under these conditions.

reactions.educational_note: Both limewater and copper oxide serve as reagents in combustion experiments but don't react with each other at room temperature.

reactions.name: Cobalt Chloride Paper + Copper Oxide — No Reaction

output.observation: No reaction. Both are solid reagents used in combustion experiments. They do not react with each other in any chemically meaningful way.

reactions.educational_note: Test reagents (cobalt chloride paper, limewater) are used to detect combustion products — they don't react with each other or with oxidants like CuO.
